The root cause of the regression was in `MultiReplace.__init__` in boltons/strutils.py. When building the combined regex for plain-string (non-regex) substitutions, the code was calling `re.escape(vals[1])` — escaping the *replacement* value — instead of `re.escape(vals[0])`, the *search* pattern. Fix applied: changed `exp = re.escape(vals[1])` to `exp = re.escape(vals[0])` so the search pattern (not the replacement) is escaped and used to build the regex.

The regression in boltons/strutils.py has been fixed. In MultiReplace.__init__, the code was erroneously escaping the replacement value (vals[1]) instead of the search pattern (vals[0]) when building the regex for plain-string substitutions. Changed `exp = re.escape(vals[1])` to `exp = re.escape(vals[0])`.

Verified via direct execution:
- multi_replace('The cat is purple', {'cat': 'kedi', 'purple': 'mor'}) -> 'The kedi is mor' (correct)
- multi_replace('The foo bar cat ate a bat', {'foo': 'zoo', 'cat': 'hat', 'bat': 'kraken'}) -> 'The zoo bar hat ate a kraken' (matches docstring)
- MultiReplace({'foo': 'baz', 'baz': 'bar'}).sub('foo bar baz') -> 'baz bar bar' (matches documented dict-ordering example)

This single-line fix restores correct behavior for all affected multi_replace use cases (shortcut function, simple substitutions, compiled-regex substitutions, and iterable/dict-based substitutions) without touching any other logic.
